meta.title: The Voices That Remain
meta.event: Opera in the Age of Everything — Annual Report 2026

cover.headline: The Voices
cover.body: Opera is in perpetual crisis. It is also, as it has always been, irrepressibly alive. This report explores what the art form is becoming — and why that matters more than ever.
cover.colophon: Produced by the Royal Opera House with Harpoon Productions

sections.title: Overture

card_image.alt: Conductor raises baton at the Royal Opera House

hero_image.alt: The Royal Opera House auditorium, seen from the stage

sections.intro: Opera was invented to resurrect something that had been lost. The Florentine Camerata, attempting to revive the drama of ancient Greece, accidentally created the most expensive, most demanding and most emotionally overwhelming art form the world has ever seen. It has been in crisis ever since. It has also never stopped.

pull_quote.text: Every generation believes it will be the last to hear a live orchestra in a great opera house. Every generation has been wrong.

sections.title: The Voice

hero_image.alt: Close detail of a singer's face in performance

sections.intro: The trained operatic voice is one of the rarest and most fragile instruments in existence. It takes a decade to form, a lifetime to master, and a single illness to silence. This section examines how the voice is made — and what the industry is doing to protect it.

sticky_steps.title: Formation
sticky_steps.body: The voice begins to mature in adolescence but rarely reaches full operatic capability before the late twenties. Most conservatoires now delay heavy repertoire training until singers are physiologically ready — a shift from the 20th-century practice of pushing voices young and fast.

image.alt: Young singers in a conservatoire vocal class

sticky_steps.title: Range and Register
sticky_steps.body: The operatic Fach system classifies voices into approximately twenty categories — from the lyric soprano to the Heldentenor to the basso profondo. A singer's Fach determines their repertoire, their career arc, and often the roles that will define them.

image.alt: Voice range diagram illustrated across a piano keyboard

sticky_steps.title: Endurance
sticky_steps.body: A dramatic soprano singing Brünnhilde in Wagner's Ring Cycle must sustain three to four hours of vocally demanding performance across four evenings. The physical demands are comparable to an elite athlete. Rest, hydration and repertoire management are not optional — they are the career.

image.alt: Soprano performing the Immolation Scene from Götterdämmerung

sticky_steps.title: Protection
sticky_steps.body: The ROH now employs a resident voice health team — laryngologists, speech therapists and physiotherapists — embedded in the rehearsal process. Vocal fatigue indicators are tracked across the season. The days of singing through illness are ending.

image.alt: Singer in consultation with the ROH voice health team

hero_image.alt: Tenor and soprano in the final act of Tosca, Castel Sant'Angelo set

pull_quote.text: Opera is the only art form in which a human being can make you weep simply by standing still and opening their mouth.

sections.title: New Works

card_image.alt: Set model for a new commission

sections.intro: This season the ROH premiered four new operas — more than any season in the past thirty years. Each one asked a different question of the form.

cards.title: Estuary
cards.body: A chamber opera for six voices set entirely on a Thames houseboat, exploring grief and inheritance across three generations of a London-Irish family. Music by Tansy Davies; libretto by Nick Drake. World premiere, Linbury Theatre, October 2025.

cards.title: Antigone
cards.body: A full-scale reworking of the Sophocles tragedy for dramatic soprano and large orchestra. Music by George Benjamin; libretto by Martin Crimp. The third collaboration between Benjamin and Crimp, following Written on Skin and Lessons in Love and Violence. Main Stage premiere, January 2026.

image.alt: Soprano as Antigone against a stark limestone set

cards.title: Salt
cards.body: An opera in one act exploring the transatlantic slave trade through the voices of those who were never recorded in the historical archive. Music by Errollyn Wallen; libretto by Lemn Sissay. Co-production with English National Opera and the Barbados National Cultural Foundation.

cards.title: The Machine Stops
cards.body: Based on E.M. Forster's 1909 short story, this digital-native opera was designed from the outset for live performance and simultaneous global broadcast. Music by Nico Muhly; libretto by Meredith Oakes. A co-production with the Metropolitan Opera, New York, and the Opéra national de Paris.

image.alt: The vast digital set of The Machine Stops

sections.title: Who Comes

card_image.alt: Audience in the ROH auditorium before curtain up

hero_image.alt: Diverse audience members in the foyer during interval

sections.intro: The question of who opera is for has haunted the form since its invention. The short answer — everyone — has never been self-evident in practice. This season, for the first time, the ROH published a full audience diversity report.

toggle_panels.label: Age
toggle_panels.body: The median age of a first-time ROH visitor fell to 34 this season — the lowest recorded figure. The under-35 audience grew by 19% year-on-year, driven by the £10 Friday Rush ticket scheme and expanded school-visit programme. The over-65 audience remains the largest single cohort at 31% of all attendances.

image.alt: Young and older audience members in conversation

toggle_panels.label: Geography
toggle_panels.body: 48% of live audience members travelled from outside Greater London this season. International visitors — attending as part of a planned trip to the UK — accounted for 22% of Main Stage attendances, reflecting London's role as a global operatic destination. Regional touring reached 14 cities.

image.alt: Map showing audience origin data across the UK

toggle_panels.label: Access
toggle_panels.body: Audio description, captioning and British Sign Language-interpreted performances are now standard across all Main Stage productions. The ROH's relaxed performances — designed for neurodivergent audience members and those with sensory sensitivities — sold out every date this season, prompting an expansion to eight performances per season from 2026–27.

contributors.name: Asmik Grigorian
contributors.title: Soprano
contributors.bio: Armenian-Lithuanian soprano Asmik Grigorian made her ROH debut this season as Violetta in a new production of La Traviata. Her Salzburg Salome is already considered one of the defining operatic performances of the 21st century.

contributors.name: Gerald Finley
contributors.title: Baritone
contributors.bio: Canadian baritone Gerald Finley returned to the ROH this season for his fifth Golaud in Pelléas et Mélisande, a role he has made definitive across three decades. He also premiered the title role in Antigone.

contributors.name: Simone Young
contributors.title: Chief Conductor
contributors.bio: Australian conductor Simone Young became the first woman to conduct the Vienna Philharmonic and the first to conduct the complete Ring cycle at the Vienna State Opera. She begins her tenure as ROH Chief Conductor in the 2026–27 season.

sections.title: Ask the Report
sections.intro: The Briefing Engine is trained on the full text of this report, the ROH's archive of production notes, and the 2025–26 season programme books. Ask it anything.

briefing_engine.title: Briefing Engine — The Voices That Remain
briefing_engine.welcome_message: Hello. I'm trained on this report and the full ROH 2025–26 season archive. You can ask me about any production, any artist, the audience data, the new commissions, or opera more broadly. What would you like to know?
suggested_questions: Which new opera premiered this season got the best reviews?
How has the ROH's under-35 audience changed in the last five years?
Tell me about the Ring Cycle and who has conducted it at Covent Garden
What is the Fach system and why does it matter?
How does the ROH compare to the Met in terms of new commissions?
Who is singing Brünnhilde next season?
